questions.question: Is (P∧(P→Q))→Q a tautology?
questions.solutionApproach: This is exactly Modus Ponens in formula form. Check: if P=T,Q=F: P→Q=F, so P∧(P→Q)=F, F→Q=T. If P=T,Q=T: P→Q=T, P∧T=T, T→T=T. If P=F: P∧(...)=F regardless, F→anything=T. All rows True.
questions.answer: Yes, it's a tautology (this is the formal statement of Modus Ponens).

questions.question: Is ¬(P→Q) equivalent to P∧¬Q?
questions.solutionApproach: P→Q ≡ ¬P∨Q. So ¬(P→Q) ≡ ¬(¬P∨Q) ≡ P∧¬Q (De Morgan's). Yes, equivalent.

questions.question: Translate: 'You can enter the exam hall only if you have your admit card.'
questions.solutionApproach: 'A only if B' → A→B. Let E=can enter, C=has admit card. Translation: E→C.

questions.question: Given premises: (1) P→Q, (2) Q→R, (3) P. Is R derivable? Show the steps.
questions.solutionApproach: From (1),(3) via Modus Ponens: Q. From (2) and Q via Modus Ponens: R. Yes, derivable (this is Hypothetical Syllogism + Modus Ponens chained).
questions.answer: Yes — R follows in two Modus Ponens steps.

questions.question: What is the CONTRAPOSITIVE of 'If it rains, the match is cancelled'? And separately, what is its CONVERSE?
questions.solutionApproach: Let R=rains, C=cancelled. Original: R→C. Contrapositive (equivalent): ¬C→¬R ('If the match is not cancelled, it did not rain'). Converse (NOT equivalent): C→R ('If the match is cancelled, it rains' — could be cancelled for other reasons, so this is a different claim).
questions.answer: Contrapositive: ¬C→¬R (equivalent to original). Converse: C→R (NOT equivalent — classic trap).
